ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, one end of the straight rod BC is fixed to a vertical wall by a hinge, and the other end is fixed with a small pulley C. The lower end of the light string hangs a heavy object, and the AC segment of the light string is horizontal. Neglect the masses of the straight rod, pulley, and light string, and ignore all friction. If the endpoint A of the light string is moved slightly downward to point A', making it reach equilibrium again, then at this time the position of pulley C is (　　)

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, on the left side there is a vertical wall; on the wall, point A is marked above, and point B is marked below; the straight rod BC connects from point B obliquely upward to the right to point C, and at C there is a small pulley; the light string is pulled horizontally from point A on the wall to point C, passes around the pulley, and then hangs the heavy object G vertically downward. Reasoning: Take B as the coordinate origin, the wall as the y-axis, and the original height of point A as h. Since AC is horizontal in the figure, the initial height of point C is also h. Pulley C is acted on by equal tensions from two segments of the string: one segment is horizontally leftward along CA, and one segment is vertically downward; straight rod BC is a weightless two-force rod, so the direction of the resultant force of these two tensions must be along CB. The initial horizontal tension and vertical tension are equal, and the resultant force makes equal angles with the horizontal and vertical, so initially AC=AB=h, and thus the rod length satisfies BC^2=AB^2+AC^2=2h^2. Move endpoint A downward to A', let the height of A' be h', and h'<h; when equilibrium is reached again, let the coordinates of C be (x,y). At this time, the rope force at C is still the tension of one segment along the direction CA' and the tension of one segment vertically downward, and the resultant force needs to be along CB. According to this equilibrium condition, CA'=A'B=h' can be obtained. The rod length is unchanged, so x^2+y^2=BC^2=2h^2; also CA'=h', so x^2+(y-h')^2=h'^2. Combining the two equations gives x^2+y^2=2h'y, that is, 2h^2=2h'y, so y=h^2/h'. Because h'<h, y>h. That is to say, after reaching equilibrium again, the height of point C is higher than the original point A. Final answer: Above point A.
